in post-absorptive humans (Ryan et al., 2021). The synthesis of glutamine from NH3 and glutamate plays a major role in removing
ammonia from the blood. Furthermore, the skeletal muscle, heart, brain, lungs, and white adipose tissue of humans can intercon-
vert serine and glycine.
The small intestine
The small intestine is the terminal site for the digestion of dietary proteins and the absorption of its products (small peptides and
free AAs). In addition, as for many other mammals, the small intestine of humans can form alanine, arginine, aspartate, asparagine,
citrulline, ornithine, and proline from glutamate and glutamine; glutamate from BCAAs plus glucose, glutamine, and proline;
glycine from serine; tyrosine from phenylalanine; and methionine from homocysteine (Wu, 2022). The gut releases alanine, argi-
nine, citrulline, ornithine, and proline in the post-absorptive state. The mammalian small intestine has a limited ability to synthe-
size glutamine due to a low activity of glutamine synthetase. Citrulline bypasses the liver and only about 10% of arginine in the
